title: US 30-Year Treasury Yield Nears Longest Stretch Above 5% Since 2007
excerpt: The benchmark long bond has stayed above 5% for 11 straight sessions, driven by renewed Middle East tensions, persistent inflation, and a wave of corporate debt issuance from AI hyperscalers.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US 30-year Treasury yield has surpassed 5% for 11 consecutive sessions, the longest since 2007.
  • A 12th session above 5% would mark a milestone not seen in 19 years.
  • Brent crude prices have risen above $90 per barrel amid geopolitical tensions.
  • AI hyperscalers have issued nearly $500 billion in long-duration corporate debt, impacting Treasuries.
  • Average 30-year fixed mortgage rates have climbed above 7.5%, affecting the housing market.
Treasury Yield Milestone
›30-year Treasury yield closed at 5.13%.
›11 consecutive sessions above 5%.
›Next milestone: 12 sessions, not seen since 2004.
›Inflation rate at 3.5%, above Fed's 2% target.

Bond Market Flashes a Warning

The US Treasury market is approaching a milestone that hasn't been seen since before the 2008 financial crisis. The 30-year Treasury yield on Tuesday closed at 5.13%, marking its 11th straight session above the psychologically significant 5% threshold, according to MarketWatch and Dow Jones Market Data. If it remains above 5% through Wednesday, it will set the longest such stretch since 2007.

The renewed selloff in the $30 trillion Treasury market comes as multiple forces converge on longer-duration bonds. The fragile US-Iran ceasefire agreement has collapsed, sending global Brent crude prices back above $90 a barrel. While inflation data eased somewhat in June, the consumer price index rate still stands at 3.5% — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target.

"The biggest enemy working against longer-duration bonds is inflation. And if inflation is going to be higher for longer, then you need to be compensated for that."

— Dustin Reid, Chief Fixed-Income Strategist, Mackenzie Investments

AI Spending Adds to the Pressure

Beyond geopolitics and inflation, the bond market faces a structural challenge. A wave of longer-duration corporate debt issuance from AI hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta, and Oracle — has pushed total outstanding debt from these companies near $500 billion in 2026, according to BondCliQ data cited by MarketWatch. This flood of high-grade corporate bonds competes directly with Treasuries for investor capital.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, testifying on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, estimated the Iran conflict has already cost $37.5 billion. The Trump administration is requesting a supplemental $67 billion to help fund the escalating conflict, adding to a US debt load that topped 100% of GDP this spring and is approaching $40 trillion.

Market Implications

The persistent elevation of long-term yields directly affects borrowing costs across the economy. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has climbed above 7.5%, pressuring the housing market. Corporate financing costs are rising, potentially dampening investment and expansion plans.

Corporate Debt Surge
›AI hyperscalers' corporate debt near $500 billion by 2026.
›Major players: Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta.
›High-grade corporate bonds compete with Treasuries.

Despite the bond market stress, equities have held up. The S&P 500 is up 9.7% year-to-date, the Dow has gained 8.7%, and the Nasdaq is up 11.2%, according to FactSet.

Fixed-income strategists are watching the 5.25% level on the 30-year yield as a potential trigger for intervention. "They don't want the back end of the Treasury curve flying away too much," said Mackenzie's Reid, warning that sustained yields at those levels "would certainly cause some risk around equities and valuations."

Market Impact Overview
›Average 30-year mortgage rate above 7.5%.
›S&P 500 up 9.7% year-to-date.
›Dow gained 8.7%, Nasdaq up 11.2%.
›Potential intervention at 5.25% yield level.

What's Next

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon recently said he "wouldn't buy Treasurys," questioning the upside case for government bonds. Wellington Management's Brij Khurana suggested domestic holders will need to replace declining foreign participation in the Treasury market — but likely only when equities weaken. For NRI investors with exposure to US fixed income or real estate, the elevated yield environment represents both higher returns on new bond purchases and increased borrowing costs for mortgages and business loans.
